Normal exercise response: HR rises about 10 beats/min per MET and returns to the pre-exercise level in 3-5 min; SBP rises about 10 mmHg per MET. Stop criteria include SBP drop >10 mmHg with increasing workload, new or worsening dysrhythmia, RR >40, unable to speak comfortably, SpO2 <90% or a drop of 4% or more (acute coronary syndrome), SpO2 <85% (lung disease); lung disease activity target 88-92%. brief.situation: 10:00 in the medical ICU. You are the physical therapist. Mrs. Okafor, 64, is on day 3 of a stay for pneumonia with sepsis and is getting better. Rounds set today's goal: out of bed to the chair.
handover: High-flow nasal cannula, 40 L/min, FiO2 0.45. Arterial line, peripheral IV.
Awake, calm, following commands. Lived alone and walked without an aid before admission.
Her nurse is in the room and can help; the respiratory therapist is on the unit.
howItWorks: The clock runs in real time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Her heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and breathing respond to each activity and recover with rest, as in a real session.
The stopping rules are on screen. A rule that is met now is marked and read out at once.
Early on you are asked to write your plan. Then a debrief scores what you did.

plan.question: Before she moves: is Mrs. Okafor safe to get out of bed today, what will you watch while she is up, and what will make you stop?

parts.label: Is it safe to start?
parts.criteria: Uses a safety screen across systems: oxygen need below the commonly used limit (FiO2 under 0.6) with SpO2 above 90% and RR under 30; no rising vasopressor dose (off for 8 h, MAP stable); awake and following commands; lines secured. Concludes she can start, with oxygen in reserve.
parts.modelAnswer: Yes. FiO2 is 0.45 with SpO2 93% and RR 24, she has been off norepinephrine for 8 hours with a stable MAP, and she is awake and following commands. I will secure the lines, have her nurse help and keep extra oxygen available.

parts.label: What to watch and when to stop
parts.criteria: Monitors HR, rhythm, BP, SpO2, RR and RPE or the talk test during each step; stages the activity (edge of bed, stand, march, chair); names stopping rules: SpO2 below about 88-90% that does not recover, a new arrhythmia, a falling SBP as work rises, RR above 40, inability to speak; and the response: sit her down, raise the oxygen with the team, call the nurse and ICU team for a new rhythm.
parts.modelAnswer: I will step her up from the edge of the bed to standing, marching, then the chair, watching the monitor and asking her RPE. I stop if SpO2 drops below 88% and does not come back with rest, if a new arrhythmia appears, if SBP drops as she works, if RR goes over 40 or if she cannot talk. Then I sit her down, ask the RT to raise the oxygen, and for a new rhythm I call her nurse and the ICU team.

expertPath.text: Chart and trends, then the safety screen with her nurse: FiO2 0.45, SpO2 93%, RR 24, off pressors 8 h, following commands. Lines secured with slack.
Edge of the bed for a minute or two, then stand at the walker with a gait belt, nurse assisting. Ask her RPE.
Marching drops her SpO2 toward 88%: sit her down, coach pursed-lip breathing and ask the RT for FiO2 0.60.
Rest until she recovers, stand again and march on the higher FiO2, then step-pivot to the chair.
After 15 minutes in the chair, hand over: what she did, the oxygen she needed, and the plan for next time.

chairSafe.headline: In the chair, inside the stopping rules
chairSafe.body: You screened before moving her, staged the activity, and acted as soon as her saturation fell: rest, breathing, more oxygen with the team. That is the expert path.

chairGaps.headline: In the chair, with gaps
chairGaps.body: She got there, which matters. Look at the safety screen and how long her saturation stayed below 88% before the activity eased.

backInBed.headline: Back in bed
backInBed.body: Safe, but the goal for today was not reached. If a new rhythm sent her back, that was the right call; if not, staging, rest and oxygen usually get a patient like her to the chair.

rapidResponse.headline: Rapid response
rapidResponse.body: The most useful kind of run to learn from. A saturation that stays under 88% during activity means sit down, rest and more oxygen; a new fast rhythm means stop and call the team at once.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: The hour ran out before the handover.

scoring.modelReasoning: Mrs. Okafor meets common safety criteria to start: FiO2 under 0.6 with SpO2 over 90% and RR under 30, no rising vasopressor (off for 8 h), awake and following commands. Secure lines, stage the activity (edge of bed, stand with a gait belt, march, step-pivot to the chair) and monitor HR, rhythm, BP, SpO2, RR and RPE. Expect HR and SBP to rise about 10 per MET and recover in 3-5 minutes. Her SpO2 falls with effort; below 88% the response is to sit, rest, coach pursed-lip breathing and ask the RT for more oxygen before trying again. A new arrhythmia is a stop rule: sit or lie her down and call the nurse and the ICU team at once.

afterRest.ask: She is resting after marching. What should her heart rate and saturation do over the next few minutes?

choices.label: Settle back toward her resting values within about 3-5 minutes
Stay where they were at the peak of the activity
Fall well below her resting values

afterRest.explain: After activity, heart rate normally returns toward its pre-exercise level within 3-5 minutes, and saturation recovers as the oxygen demand falls. A rate or saturation that does not recover with rest is a reason to stop for the day and tell the team.

nextTime.ask: Next session, what would most likely keep her SpO2 at or above 88% while she marches?

choices.label: Plan the oxygen increase and rest breaks with the RT before she stands
March for longer so she gets used to it
Skip standing and keep her in bed until she is off oxygen

nextTime.explain: Oxygen reserve should exceed the activity, and an activity target of 88-92% is usual in lung disease. Planning the oxygen and the rest breaks lets her keep moving, which is the point of early mobility.
